sb-auth.md:
## Why it exists
Every app needs sign-up, sign-in, password reset and sessions, and home-made versions are full of security holes. **Supabase Auth** is a managed service that handles these and issues signed tokens your database can trust.

{{dg:0}}

## How it works
Signing in returns a **session**: a short-lived **access token** (a JWT) and a long-lived **refresh token**. The client sends the access token with each request, and the API turns its claims into Postgres settings, which is how `auth.uid()` works inside RLS policies. Refresh tokens are single-use: each refresh issues a new pair.

## Worked example
```ts
// sign up and sign in
await supabase.auth.signUp({ email, password })
const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.signInWithPassword({ email, password })

// OAuth and magic links use the same session mechanism
await supabase.auth.signInWithOAuth({ provider: 'github' })
await supabase.auth.signInWithOtp({ email })
```

## The server-side rule that matters
| Method | What it does | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `getClaims()` | Verifies the JWT: locally against cached public keys with asymmetric signing keys, otherwise via the Auth server | Protecting pages, routes and data |
| `getUser()` | Asks the Auth server on every call and returns the latest user record | Fresh user data, revocation checks |
| `getSession()` | Reads the session from cookies with no verification | Getting tokens; never for authorization decisions |

```ts
// server code: route handler, server action, middleware
const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.getClaims()
if (error || !data?.claims) redirect('/login')
const userId = data.claims.sub
```

## SSR frameworks
Server-rendered apps (Next.js, SvelteKit, Remix) need cookie-based sessions so the server can see who is signed in. Use the `@supabase/ssr` package: a browser client for client components, a server client that reads and writes cookies, and middleware that refreshes the session on each request. It replaces the older auth-helpers packages.

## In real products
- Social login plus email magic links reduces password support.
- Add MFA (TOTP) and require it for sensitive tables with `(select auth.jwt()->>'aal') = 'aal2'` in the policy.
- Auth hooks let you add custom claims, such as a tenant or role, to the token at sign-in.
- Keep roles in `app_metadata` or your own tables, never in `user_metadata`.

> [!pitfall] Trusting getSession() in server code lets a forged cookie pass as a user. Verify with getClaims() or getUser().
> [!security] A JWT stays valid until it expires, even if you ban the user. Keep access tokens short-lived and use getUser() where freshness matters.
> [!tip] New projects use asymmetric JWT signing keys by default. On projects still using the legacy shared secret, getClaims() calls the Auth server just like getUser().
q: Why is getSession() unsafe for authorization in server code?
It reads the session from cookies without verifying the token, so a tampered cookie could be trusted.
When would you pick getUser() over getClaims()?
When you need the latest user record or must catch a revoked or banned user, since getUser() asks the Auth server every time.
res: How claims are verified and when it falls back to the server

sb-overview.md:
## Why it exists
Most apps need the same backend pieces: a database, user accounts, file storage, live updates and a place to run server code. **Supabase** bundles them around one open-source **Postgres** database, so you keep standard SQL and your data stays portable.

{{dg:0}}

## The pieces
| Product | What it is | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Database | A full Postgres instance per project | Your tables, SQL, extensions |
| Auto API (PostgREST) | REST API generated from your schema | `supabase.from('todos').select()` |
| Auth | Users, sessions, OAuth, MFA | Sign-in; issues JWTs |
| Storage | Files in buckets with Postgres-based access rules | Avatars, uploads |
| Realtime | Live database changes, broadcast and presence | Chat, live cursors |
| Edge Functions | Server-side TypeScript on Deno | Webhooks, secrets, AI calls |

## How a request flows
The browser sends the user's JWT with the request. The API layer turns it into a Postgres role and claims, and **Row Level Security** policies decide which rows come back. There is no separate authorization server in the middle: the database enforces the rules.

{{dg:1}}

## Worked example
```ts
import { createClient } from '@supabase/supabase-js'

const supabase = createClient(
  'https://YOUR-PROJECT.supabase.co',
  'sb_publishable_...' // safe in the browser; RLS is what protects the data
)

const { data, error } = await supabase
  .from('todos')
  .select('id, title, done')
  .eq('done', false)
  .order('id', { ascending: false })
  .limit(20)
```

## Keys: the part people get wrong
- **Publishable key** (`sb_publishable_...`) goes in browser and mobile code. It carries low privileges, and your RLS policies decide what it can see. It replaces the legacy `anon` key.
- **Secret key** (`sb_secret_...`) is server-only. It maps to the `service_role` Postgres role, which **bypasses RLS**. It replaces the legacy `service_role` key.
- Supabase is deprecating the legacy JWT-based `anon` and `service_role` keys by the end of 2026. Creating new keys does not revoke the old ones, so migrate deliberately and check every place a key is stored.

> [!pitfall] Shipping the secret or service_role key in front-end code gives every visitor full database access. Keep it in server environment variables only.
> [!tip] Enable RLS on every table in the public schema, then write policies. A table with RLS off and the API exposed is readable by anyone holding the publishable key.
> [!prod] Local development: `supabase start` runs the whole stack in Docker, and the files in `supabase/migrations` replay the same schema in every environment.
q: Which key is safe to put in browser code, and what protects your data when you do?
The publishable key; Row Level Security policies decide what it can read or write.
Why does the secret key need to stay on the server?
It maps to the service_role role, which bypasses RLS and can read and change everything.

sb-pgvector.md:
## Why it exists
Search by meaning, not keywords: a question about cancelling a plan should find a page titled ending your subscription. **Embeddings** turn text into vectors, and **pgvector** lets Postgres store and search them next to your other data, with the same RLS and backups.

{{dg:0}}

## How it works
An embedding model maps text to an array of floats (for example 1,536 numbers). Similar meanings land near each other. A query is embedded the same way, and Postgres returns the rows with the smallest distance. For large tables an approximate index such as **HNSW** keeps search fast.

## Worked example
```sql
create extension if not exists vector;

create table public.documents (
  id bigint generated always as identity primary key,
  tenant_id uuid not null,
  content text not null,
  embedding vector(1536)
);

create index on public.documents using hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);

-- nearest 5 chunks to a query embedding ($1)
select id, content, 1 - (embedding <=> $1) as similarity
from public.documents
order by embedding <=> $1
limit 5;
```
`<=>` is cosine distance, `<->` is L2 distance and `<#>` is negative inner product. Use the operator that matches your index's operator class and your embedding model's recommended metric.

## In a RAG app
1. Chunk documents into a few hundred tokens each, with some overlap.
2. Embed each chunk and insert it with its metadata.
3. On a question, embed it, search, and pass the top chunks to the LLM along with the question.
4. Filter by tenant or user. RLS applies to vector queries too, so one customer's chunks never reach another.

## Trade-offs
| Choice | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| HNSW index | Fast, high recall, no training step | Slower builds, more memory |
| IVFFlat index | Smaller, faster to build | Needs data first; tune lists and probes |
| Exact scan (no index) | Perfect recall | Slow on big tables |
| Hybrid (vectors plus full-text) | Better recall on names and codes | More moving parts |

> [!pitfall] The vector dimension is fixed per column. Changing embedding models means re-embedding everything, so record the model name next to each row.
> [!tip] Combine vector search with a Postgres full-text query and merge the results. Pure semantic search can miss exact identifiers such as error codes.
> [!cost] Embedding calls and storage grow with your corpus. Cache embeddings and re-embed only the chunks that changed.
q: Why record the embedding model name alongside each row?
Vectors from different models are not comparable and dimensions can differ, so you need to know which rows to re-embed when you switch.
What does the HNSW index trade away for speed?
Exact results and build time or memory: it returns approximate nearest neighbours.

sb-rls.md:
## Why it exists
With Supabase the browser talks to the database API directly, so there is no backend code to say that a user may only read their own rows. **Row Level Security (RLS)** moves that rule into Postgres itself: every query is filtered by policies, no matter which client sends it.

{{dg:0}}

## How it works
1. Enable RLS on a table. With no policies, nobody except roles that bypass RLS can read or write it.
2. Add policies. Each applies to a command (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) and a role.
3. `USING` filters which existing rows are visible or modifiable. `WITH CHECK` validates new or changed rows.
4. `auth.uid()` returns the signed-in user's id from the JWT.

## Worked example
```sql
create table public.todos (
  id bigint generated always as identity primary key,
  user_id uuid not null default auth.uid() references auth.users(id) on delete cascade,
  title text not null,
  done boolean not null default false
);
alter table public.todos enable row level security;

create policy todos_select_own on public.todos
  for select to authenticated
  using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);

create policy todos_insert_own on public.todos
  for insert to authenticated
  with check ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);

create policy todos_update_own on public.todos
  for update to authenticated
  using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id)
  with check ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);

create policy todos_delete_own on public.todos
  for delete to authenticated
  using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);

create index on public.todos (user_id);
```
Wrapping the call as `(select auth.uid())` lets Postgres evaluate it once per query instead of once per row; Supabase's own benchmarks show large gains. `to authenticated` stops the policy from running for signed-out requests, and the index on `user_id` keeps the filter fast.

## Roles and bypass
| Key and state | Postgres role | RLS applies? |
|---|---|---|
| Publishable key, signed out | anon | Yes: public content only |
| Publishable key, signed in | authenticated | Yes: normal users |
| Secret key | service_role | No, it has BYPASSRLS: trusted server code only |

## Multi-tenant pattern
```sql
create table public.memberships (
  tenant_id uuid, user_id uuid, role text,
  primary key (tenant_id, user_id)
);

create function public.is_member(t uuid) returns boolean
  language sql security definer set search_path = '' stable as $$
  select exists (
    select 1 from public.memberships m
    where m.tenant_id = t and m.user_id = (select auth.uid())
  );
$$;

create policy docs_member_read on public.documents
  for select to authenticated
  using ((select public.is_member(tenant_id)));
```
A `security definer` helper avoids the policy re-triggering RLS on `memberships`, and `set search_path = ''` closes a classic privilege-escalation hole.

## Testing policies
Impersonate a user inside a transaction and check what comes back:
```sql
begin;
set local role authenticated;
select set_config('request.jwt.claims', '{"sub":"00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001"}', true);
select * from public.todos;   -- should show only that user's rows
rollback;
```

> [!pitfall] Never base authorization on user_metadata: signed-in users can edit it. Use app_metadata, which only the server controls, or a membership table.
> [!pitfall] Views run with the view owner's rights by default and can bypass RLS. On Postgres 15 and later create them with security_invoker = true.
> [!pitfall] UPDATE typically needs a matching SELECT policy, because Postgres must be able to read the row it changes.
> [!tip] Index every column your policies filter on, and avoid joins inside policies. Use a security definer function or an IN (select ...) subquery instead.
q: What is the difference between USING and WITH CHECK?
USING filters rows that already exist; WITH CHECK validates the row being inserted or the new version being written by an update.
Why write (select auth.uid()) instead of auth.uid() in a policy?
The select wrapper makes Postgres evaluate the function once per query and cache the result, instead of once for every row checked.
Can a request made with the secret key be blocked by RLS?
No. The secret key maps to service_role, which has BYPASSRLS.

sb-storage-realtime.md:
## Why it exists
Apps need files (avatars, uploads), live updates (chat, presence) and a safe place for server code that cannot run in the browser (secrets, webhooks). Supabase covers each with a product that reuses your Postgres users and policies.

{{dg:0}}

## Storage
Files live in **buckets**, and each file also has a row in `storage.objects`, so access control is just RLS policies.
```ts
await supabase.storage.from('avatars').upload(`${userId}/me.png`, file, { upsert: true })
const { data } = await supabase.storage.from('avatars').createSignedUrl(`${userId}/me.png`, 3600)
```
```sql
create policy avatars_owner_read on storage.objects
  for select to authenticated
  using (bucket_id = 'avatars' and (select auth.uid())::text = (storage.foldername(name))[1]);
```
Public buckets serve files to anyone with the URL. Private buckets need policies or signed URLs. Name files inside a folder per user id so policies can match the path.

## Realtime
Three features over WebSockets: **Postgres Changes** (rows inserted, updated or deleted), **Broadcast** (low-latency messages between clients) and **Presence** (who is online and shared state).
```ts
supabase.channel('room-1')
  .on('postgres_changes', { event: 'INSERT', schema: 'public', table: 'messages' },
      (payload) => console.log('new message', payload.new))
  .subscribe()
```
To receive Postgres Changes, add the table to the `supabase_realtime` publication. Changes are filtered by RLS, so users only receive rows they may read. Use Broadcast for high-frequency data such as cursors and typing, because it skips the database.

## Edge Functions
Server-side TypeScript running on Deno close to your users. Use them for webhooks, calling third-party APIs with secret keys, and AI calls.
```ts
Deno.serve(async (req) => {
  const { name } = await req.json()
  return new Response(JSON.stringify({ message: `Hello ${name}` }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } })
})
```
Call it with `supabase.functions.invoke('hello', { body: { name: 'Ana' } })`. Secrets are set with the CLI and read with `Deno.env.get`. Edge Functions support npm modules and Node built-in APIs.

## Choosing
| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Store a user file | Storage |
| Show new rows live | Realtime Postgres Changes |
| Typing indicators, cursors | Realtime Broadcast and Presence |
| Call Stripe or an LLM with a secret | Edge Function |
| Heavy, long-running work | A queue plus a worker, not an Edge Function |

> [!pitfall] A public bucket exposes every file in it by URL. Put anything private in a private bucket with policies.
> [!pitfall] Forgetting to add the table to the Realtime publication means subscriptions connect but never receive events.
> [!security] Verify webhook signatures inside Edge Functions before acting on a payload.
q: How do you restrict a private file to its owner?
Put it under a folder named for the user id and write a storage.objects policy comparing (select auth.uid()) to the first folder segment.
Why use Broadcast instead of Postgres Changes for cursor positions?
Cursors update many times a second; Broadcast sends messages between clients directly without writing to the database.
res: Buckets, policies, signed URLs and uploads
